summary: Specifies the RTP payload format for ITU-T G.711.0, a lossless, stateless compression for G.711 packet payloads. It also defines a storage mode format and a media type registration.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a way to pack phone-call audio into smaller boxes without losing any sound.

questions: how to carry g.711.0 audio over rtp
what is the g.711.0 storage format
what sdp parameters does g.711.0 use
subtitle: How to carry losslessly compressed telephone-quality audio in RTP packets, and how to store it in files.

tldr.problem: G.711 voice payloads in VoIP are sent uncompressed, but ITU-T G.711.0 can compress them losslessly and needs an RTP payload format to be used on IP networks.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload holds one or more self-describing G.711.0 frames, optionally followed by 0x00 padding octets, with a dynamic payload type, SDP parameters such as complaw, and a simple storage file format.
tldr.outcome: The compressed audio decodes to exactly the original G.711 samples, so compression can be applied on any hop with no loss of quality. The RFC registers the audio/G711-0 media type.

facts.label: Compressed frame size
facts.value: 1 to X+1 octets for X input octets

today: RFC 7655 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It registers the audio/G711-0 media type.

sections.title: What G.711.0 Is
sections.content:
ITU-T G.711.0 is a lossless and stateless compression for G.711 packet payloads. G.711 is the benchmark standard for narrowband telephony. G.711.0 is not a codec in the usual lossy sense, but it is negotiated as if it were one, and the RFC uses both terms depending on context.

Because it is lossless and stateless, it can be used end-to-end or anywhere between systems that negotiated G.711. A G.711 RTP packet can be turned into a G.711.0 packet by compressing the payload, changing the payload type and copying the other RTP header fields, and back again with no difference. The RFC notes that this can be repeated on multiple hops with no degradation of quality.

Its design attributes include greater than 50% average compression for speech-like signals in service provider environments, being lossless for any valid G.711 payload (even modem or fax data), no dependence on earlier frames, and support for both A-law and mu-law. Input frames are 40, 80, 160, 240 or 320 samples, and a compressed frame is 1 to X+1 octets for X input octets, so the worst case grows by one octet.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like squeezing a sleeping bag into a stuff sack. When you unpack it, it is exactly the same bag. Each sack also has a label saying how big the bag is.

sections.title: The RTP Header and Payload
sections.content:
The RTP header fields are used as for G.711 (RFC 3550, RFC 3551). The main difference is that the payload type MUST be a dynamic value assigned to the flow. The static values 0 and 8 used for G.711 MUST NOT be used for G.711.0, except in rare cases of payload type exhaustion. Voice Activity Detection SHOULD NOT be used, because G.711.0 already compresses silence well. If it is used, the marker bit MUST be set on the first packet of a talkspurt.

The payload is one or more G.711.0 frames concatenated, followed by zero or more 0x00 padding octets. The first octet of each frame is a prefix code that tells the decoder how many G.711 symbols it holds (0, 40, 80, 160, 240 or 320). Frames in one payload may cover different durations, so the total time can be any multiple of 5 ms, and it MUST match the signaled ptime when SDP is used. All decoders MUST support the multiple-frame case, and no negotiation is needed for it.

A 20 ms payload of 160 octets can be encoded as 1, 2, 3 or 4 frames in six combinations, such as one 20 ms frame or 10 ms plus two 5 ms frames. Implementers are expected to use either the simplest one-frame encoding or whichever combination compresses best.
sections.plainLanguage: One packet is a row of little packed boxes, each labeled with how much sound is inside. Extra blank spacer pieces can be added and are simply ignored.

sections.title: Decoding a Payload
sections.content:
The decoding heuristic walks through the payload. It starts with counters at zero, reads at most 321 octets (the largest possible frame) into a buffer, and checks the first octet. A 0x00 octet is padding and is skipped. Anything else is passed to the G.711.0 decoder, which reads the prefix code, produces the symbols and reports how many octets it consumed. This repeats until every payload octet has been processed.

If SDP signaled a ptime and the decoded symbol count does not match it, the packet MUST be discarded unless other system knowledge allows otherwise. If a buffer does not start with a valid prefix code or padding octet, a framing error results and output known to be wrong MUST be discarded. Because reads are bounded to 321 octets, there is no buffer overrun risk.

For multiple channels, each channel is encoded into its own run of frames (a channel superframe) and the superframes are concatenated in channel order, with any padding RECOMMENDED after the last one. All channels MUST cover the same time span. If the symbol count is not a multiple of the channel count, the packet SHOULD be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver opens the boxes one at a time, reads each label, throws away the blank spacers, and checks that the total amount of sound is what it expected.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The registered media type is audio/G711-0. The required parameters are the clock rate (default 8000) and complaw, given on the a=fmtp line as al for A-law or mu for mu-law. Optional parameters are channels (MUST be present when greater than one, default 1), ptime (RECOMMENDED) and maxptime.

In SDP, the subtype goes in a=rtpmap and the remaining parameters go in a=fmtp. For offer/answer (RFC 3264), an answerer that cannot support the offered channel count MUST answer with the highest count it can support, and an answerer that cannot support an offered ptime or maxptime MUST include its own value.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the call, each side says which kind of audio squeezing it uses and how much sound goes in each packet, so both agree on how to unpack it.

sections.title: Storage Mode
sections.content:
For archiving recorded streams, the RFC defines a storage format: a magic number, a version octet and the concatenated G.711.0 frames. The magic number is the ASCII string #!G7110A\n for A-law or #!G7110M\n for mu-law. The version octet is 0x00, the only version this RFC defines, and a decoder that sees another version MUST NOT pass the rest to the G.711.0 decoder.

Gaps are filled in one of two ways. A PLC frame is made by running packet loss concealment, then compressing the result, which suits recordings such as voicemail. An erasure frame is a frame whose samples are all one of the two levels next to analog zero, so it plays back as muted and avoids fabricating audio. Both look like ordinary frames in the file. Version 0 supports a single channel only.
sections.plainLanguage: Saving a call to a file works the same way: a label saying what kind of file it is, then the packed boxes in order. If a piece of the call was lost, you either patch it with made-up sound or leave a quiet spot.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The usual RTP security considerations apply, and applications SHOULD use strong security mechanisms. Since compression is applied end-to-end, any encryption needs to be done after compression. The decoder has a finite worst-case path and never reads beyond a 321-octet buffer, so a payload carries no active content and the RFC knows of no denial-of-service attack through decoding.

G.711.0 is variable bit rate. The RFC discusses research showing that some speech codecs leak phrases through packet lengths, and argues G.711.0 is not expected to share that weakness. It does note that silence is easy to spot as frames of one or a few octets, and suggests statistically variable padding if that matters.

On congestion, G.711.0 has no means of lowering its bit rate beyond its compression, except that padding can be varied.
sections.plainLanguage: Lock the box after you pack it, not before, or it will not squeeze. Very small boxes tell a watcher that nobody was talking, so you can add filler to hide that.
